subject: chemistry
title: Reaction types and mechanisms
key_idea: Organic reactions are sorted into types, such as addition, substitution and elimination. A mechanism shows how bonds break and form. A bond can break **homolytically** to give radicals, or **heterolytically** to give ions, and curly arrows show the movement of electron pairs.

blocks.text: Most organic reactions fit one of a small number of types. Naming the type tells you what happens to the molecule.

rows: Two molecules join to form one. A C=C bond usually becomes C–C.
One atom or group is replaced by another.
A small molecule, such as HX or H₂O, is removed to leave a double bond.
A bond is broken by reaction with water, or with hydroxide ions.
Two molecules join and a small molecule, usually water, is lost.
Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
Many small monomers join to form a long chain.

items: In equations for organic redox reactions, **[O]** stands for one oxygen atom from an oxidising agent.
**[H]** stands for one hydrogen atom from a reducing agent.
Ethanol to ethanal is written CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O.
Learn the eight types and what each does to the molecule.
Addition joins, elimination removes a small molecule, substitution swaps one group for another.
[O] and [H] let you balance organic redox equations.

blocks.text: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. It can break evenly or unevenly, and which way decides what is formed.

items.meaning: A covalent bond breaks and each atom takes one electron from the pair, forming two radicals.
A covalent bond breaks and one atom takes both electrons from the pair, forming a positive ion and a negative ion.
A species with an unpaired electron. It is shown with a dot, as in Cl• and CH₃•.

rows: Ultraviolet light or high temperature, in a non-polar setting
A polar bond, often in a polar solvent

items: A radical is **very reactive**, because it has an unpaired electron.
Radical dots must be shown on every species with a single unpaired electron.
In heterolytic fission, the more electronegative atom takes both electrons of the bond and becomes negative.
Homolytic fission gives two radicals, heterolytic fission gives two ions.
A radical has an unpaired electron, shown as a dot.

blocks.text: Reactions between polar molecules and ions are described by what attacks and what is attacked. Curly arrows record the electron movement.

items.meaning: An electron-pair donor. It is attracted to a positive or partly positive carbon, such as OH⁻, CN⁻ and NH₃.
An electron-pair acceptor. It is attracted to a region of high electron density, such as the C=C bond.

items: A **curly arrow** shows the movement of a pair of electrons.
Its tail starts at a **bond or a lone pair**, or at a negative charge. It never starts at an atom or at a positive charge.
Its head shows where the pair ends up: a new bond, or on an atom as a lone pair.
To show a bond breaking, the arrow starts at the bond and points to the atom that takes both electrons.
Show any relevant partial charges (dipoles), such as δ+ on carbon in C–Br, on the structure.

diagram.alt: A sorting task: decide whether each species is a nucleophile or an electrophile.
diagram.prompt: Sort each species into nucleophile or electrophile.

items: A nucleophile donates an electron pair, an electrophile accepts one.
Curly arrows start from a bond or a lone pair, and show the movement of an electron pair.

blocks.text: A mechanism is named by what attacks and what type of reaction it is. The four main ones are listed here.

items: In a radical mechanism the steps are shown as equations. Curly arrows are not used.
The three stages of a radical mechanism are **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**.
In every other mechanism, show each curly arrow, the structures involved and any lone pairs used.
The name of a mechanism says what attacks and what kind of change happens.
Radical mechanisms are written as equations, other mechanisms use curly arrows.

checks.q: Name the type of reaction: CH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + HBr.
Explain the difference between homolytic and heterolytic fission, using Cl–Cl and H–Br as examples.
checks.a: In homolytic fission each atom takes one electron from the bond pair, so Cl–Cl gives two Cl• radicals. In heterolytic fission one atom takes both electrons, so H–Br gives H⁺ and Br⁻.

checks.q: State where a curly arrow starts and what it represents.
checks.a: It starts from a bond or a lone pair of electrons (or a negative charge), and it represents the movement of a pair of electrons.

blocks.text: Half curly arrows, which show the movement of single electrons, are not required.

items: Dots are required wherever there is a single unpaired electron, as in Cl• and CH₃•.
Dots are not required for diradicals, such as an oxygen atom shown as O.
Include every relevant dipole in a mechanism diagram.

blocks.text: This course asks for the reaction types by name.

items: Classify reactions as addition, elimination, substitution, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation.
Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond forms ions.
A radical is a species with an unpaired electron, represented in mechanisms by a single dot.
Write balanced equations for the steps of a free-radical mechanism.
In the other mechanisms, a new bond is shown by a curly arrow starting from a lone pair or from another covalent bond.
A bond breaking is shown by a curly arrow starting at the bond.
Outline mechanisms by drawing the species and curly arrows for the movement of electron pairs.
Use the full set of terms: saturated and unsaturated, homolytic and heterolytic fission, initiation, propagation and termination, nucleophile and electrophile, and nucleophilic and electrophilic.
Use the terms addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis and condensation, and oxidation and reduction.
A free radical has one or more unpaired electrons.
Name mechanisms as free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, nucleophilic substitution and nucleophilic addition.
Saturated means single carbon–carbon bonds only. Unsaturated means multiple carbon–carbon bonds are present.
Initiation forms radicals, propagation is a step where a radical reacts to make a new radical, and termination is where two radicals join to end the chain.
